The paper proposes a novel active-flow-control (AFC) strategy for bluff bodies to hide their hydrodynamic traces from predators.
A group of windward-suction-leeward-blowing (WSLB) actuators are used to control the wake of a circular cylinder submerged in a uniform flow.
An array of 33 velocity sensors are deployed in the near wake to provide feedback signals to the controller.
Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) is used to train effective control strategies for the WSLB actuation to mitigate the cylinder's hydrodynamic signatures.
Only a 0.29% deficit in streamwise velocity is detected after the control, which is a 99.5% reduction from the uncontrolled value.

The same control strategy is also effective when the cylinder undergoes transverse vortex-induced vibration (VIV), reducing the velocity deficit by 96.5% in the locked-in case and 95.9% in the unlocked-in case.
The cylinder's diameter-based Reynolds number is fixed at Re = 100, where asymmetric vortices will periodically shed from the cylinder.
The mass ratio (m*) and the reduced velocity (U_R) are used to characterize the cylinder's dynamics.
Five pairs of WSLB actuators are used, located azimuthally at θ = ±80°, ±40°, and 0° around the cylinder.
The cost function J consists of the velocity deficit and the energy consumed by the WSLB actuators.
The proximal policy optimization (PPO) algorithm is used to train the DRL agent through stochastic trial-and-error.
The learnt control strategy from the stationary cylinder scenario is directly applied as the starting point for the VIV cylinder scenario.
The control strategy effectively suppresses the VIV of the cylinder in both the locked-in and unlocked-in situations.
Vortex shedding can still be observed in the controlled VIV cases, but the strong hydrodynamic signature is constrained in the near wake.
The findings from this study can shed light on the design and operation of underwater structures and robotics to achieve hydrodynamic stealth.
